Brazil.text: Its first coffee bush was planted in Pará in 1727; today it grows about a third of the world's coffee.
Brazil.evidence: Brazil produces about a third of the world's coffee, making the country by far the world's largest producer. ... The first coffee bush in Brazil was planted by Francisco de Melo Palheta in Pará in 1727.

Vietnam.text: French missionaries are believed to have brought the coffee plant here in 1857.
Vietnam.evidence: It is believed that the coffee plant was first introduced to Vietnam in 1857 by French missionaries, but the first coffee plantations were only set up in 1888 at the Ninh Bình and Quảng Bình provinces of Tonkin.

Indonesia.text: In 1711 the Dutch East India Company shipped the first coffee from Java to Europe.
Indonesia.evidence: The plants grew, and in 1711 the first exports were sent from Java to Europe by the Dutch East India Company

Colombia.text: Its "Coffee Cultural Landscape" was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2011.
Colombia.evidence: In 2011, UNESCO declared the "Coffee Cultural Landscape" of Colombia a World Heritage Site.

Ethiopia.text: Legend says the goat herder Kaldi found coffee when it energized his flock; the story was first written in 1671.
Ethiopia.evidence: According to legend, the 9th-century goat herder Kaldi discovered the coffee plant after noticing the energizing effect the plant had on his flock, but this story did not appear in writing until 1671.

Honduras.text: In 1894 it grew 20,000 quintals of coffee and exported only a tenth of it.
Honduras.evidence: The production of coffee in 1894 was reckoned at 20,000 quintals, of which only 10 per cent was exported.

Uganda.text: Coffee is its top-earning export; in 1989 much of it was still smuggled out to sell in neighbouring countries.
Uganda.evidence: Coffee is Uganda's top-earning export crop. ... In 1989 Uganda's coffee production capacity exceeded its quota of 2.3 million bags, but ... large amounts of coffee beans were still being smuggled out of Uganda for sale in neighbouring countries.

Peru.text: Its first coffee exports, to Germany and England, only began in 1887.
Peru.evidence: The first exports of coffee, to Germany and England, did not begin until 1887.

India.text: A saint, Baba Budan, is said to have smuggled seven coffee beans from Yemen in his beard in the 1600s.
India.evidence: In the Indian context, coffee growing started at the beginning of the 17th century, with an Indian Muslim saint, Baba Budan, who, while returning from a pilgrimage to Mecca, smuggled seven coffee beans (by hiding them in his beard), from Mokha, Yemen, to Mysore in India.

Guatemala.text: Before coffee took over, 93% of its exports in 1850 were cochineal, a red dye made from crushed insects.
Guatemala.evidence: In 1850, for example, 93% of the colony's exports were in cochineal, the natural red dye created from the dried and crushed bugs of the coccidae family of scale insects.
